newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia in strong position for NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia in strong position for NATO entry.

text.p: Slovenia is well placed to become a full member of NATO in the first wave of ex-communist states to join the military alliance, a senior NATO official said on Thursday.

Deputy secretary-general Sergio Balanzino, in Ljubljana for a two-day NATO steering committee meeting, said Slovenia's admission to the alliance would pose no threat to Russia. Moscow has been a vocal opponent of NATO's eastward expansion.
"Slovenia...does not present any problem as far as NATO-Russian relations are concerned," Balanzino told a news conference.
He praised Slovenia's military evolution and encouraged the former Yugoslav republic to keep NATO's 16 members informed on the development of its young democracy and market economy.
"I expect NATO foreign ministers will identify potential new members at their meeting in December," Balanzino said.
A final decision would probably be taken at a summit of heads of state next summer, he added.
Diplomats have said Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovenia are front-runners for NATO membership.

Balazino's comments were regarded as the strongest suggestion yet that Ljubljana might qualify for NATO entry next year. The country is placed in a strategic position to the north of the volatile Balkan peninsula.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said during a visit to Ljubljana in May that 1996 would be a decisive year for Slovenia in its drive to join the alliance. But he declined to specify when the Alpine republic might become a full member.
An opinion poll in April showed three-quarters of Slovenians supporting NATO entry but half opposed having a NATO base in the country.

Slovenia's foreign ministry welcomed NATO's decision to hold its steering committee meeting in Ljubljana. "(It is) a sign of trust in current and future relations between Slovenia and NATO," said foreign ministry official Ignac Golob.

Balanzino said NATO had decided to hold some meetings in partner countries but could not say why Slovenia had been chosen as the site of the first steering committee meeting to be held outside Brussels.
Slovenia joined NATO's Partnership for Peace programme in 1993, two years after declaring independence from the former Yugoslavia.
